shared_context.statement_nl: For every integer m >= 2 and every integer g >= 0, the number N(m, g) of numerical semigroups with multiplicity m and genus g satisfies N(m, g) <= N(m, g + 1).

payload.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2 and let g be an integer with g >= 0. Define K_{m,g} to be the set of all tuples x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers such that for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}, and such that x_1 + ... + x_{m-1} = g. Define K_{m,g+1} to be the set of all tuples y = (y_1,...,y_{m-1}) of positive integers such that for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then y_i + y_j >= y_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then y_i + y_j + 1 >= y_{i+j-m}, and such that y_1 + ... + y_{m-1} = g + 1. Then there exists an injective function J_{m,g} from K_{m,g} to K_{m,g+1}.

result_payload.proof_summary: I could not complete a rigorous proof of the existence of an injective map J_{m,g}: K_{m,g} -> K_{m,g+1} from the tuple inequalities alone. I found a plausible partial idea: if k is an index where x_k is minimal among the coordinates of x, then x+e_k always still satisfies the defining inequalities, so every x in K_{m,g} has at least one 'incrementable' coordinate. However, the obvious deterministic choices (such as incrementing the first minimal coordinate, last minimal coordinate, smallest incrementable coordinate, etc.) can collide, and I was not able to construct a collision-free canonical rule or another cardinality argument that is justified solely from the given self-contained definition of K_{m,g}.

suspected_gaps: I do not have a rigorous injective construction.
I do not have an independent counting/cardinality proof that |K_{m,g}| <= |K_{m,g+1}| from the stated inequalities alone.
A natural partial lemma is provable: any coordinate attaining the minimum value is incrementable, but this does not by itself yield injectivity.

result_payload.stuck_point: The main obstruction is injectivity. I can show that for any x in K_{m,g}, if k satisfies x_k=min(x_1,...,x_{m-1}), then y=x+e_k lies in K_{m,g+1}: for any defining inequality with right-hand side k, the left side is a sum of two positive coordinates each at least x_k, hence at least x_k+1 in the i+j<m case and at least x_k in the i+j>m case, exactly what is needed after increasing x_k by 1. But different x can produce the same y under natural canonical choices, and I could not repair this.
